prompt: What does undecidability of the general halting problem mean?

answers.text: No algorithm always terminates and correctly decides, for every program and input, whether that program halts.
answers.explanation: Undecidability rules out a total, universally correct decider. Particular programs can still be analyzed, and simulation recognizes halting when it occurs.
Many programs halt; the obstacle is a universal decision procedure.

answers.text: No specific program can be proved to halt.
answers.explanation: Termination can be proved for many particular programs.
Simulation is possible, but it may itself run forever when the simulated program does.

answers.text: Every halting question requires exponential time.
answers.explanation: Undecidability is stronger than an exponential lower bound: no total decider exists.

answers.text: There is no algorithm that recognizes halting cases.
answers.explanation: Simulation recognizes a halting case by eventually observing termination.

answers.text: Only very large programs can fail to halt.
answers.explanation: Even a tiny unconditional infinite loop need not halt.

answers.text: A decider exists if it may take arbitrarily long but finite time on every input.
answers.explanation: That would still be a total decision algorithm, which undecidability rules out.

answers.text: No restricted programming language has a decidable halting problem.
answers.explanation: Some restricted languages or finite-state systems do have decidable halting problems.

answers.text: Simulation decides both halting and nonhalting by waiting long enough.
answers.explanation: Any finite wait is inconclusive when a program has not halted yet; it may halt later.
